hints: Look at what has been added to benzene in step 1, a $C(CH_3)_3$ tert-butyl group, and recall which type of benzene reaction adds an alkyl group.
Think about what pair of reagents generates the alkyl electrophile for that reaction, a chloroalkane plus a specific aluminium chloride catalyst.
walkthrough:
Spot the alkyl group added**
You start with benzene, $C_6H_6$, and you end step 1 with $C_6H_5C(CH_3)_3$, tert-butylbenzene. A hydrogen on the ring has been replaced by a bulky alkyl group. That is the classic Friedel-Crafts alkylation, an electrophilic substitution on the benzene ring.

Pick the electrophile source and catalyst**
To put a $(CH_3)_3C$ group on, you need the electrophile $(CH_3)_3C^+$. Get it from 2-chloro-2-methylpropane, $(CH_3)_3CCl$, with anhydrous $AlCl_3$ catalyst (2-methylpropene, $(CH_3)_2C=CH_2$, also works). Heat is needed to sustain the reaction.

Final answer: reagents: $(CH_3)_3CCl$ (or $(CH_3)_2C=CH_2$) and $AlCl_3$
conditions: heat

hints: Notice step 2 uses $Cl_2(g)$ on an alkylbenzene but the product H shows the ring is unchanged, so decide whether this is ring chlorination or side-chain chlorination.
walkthrough:
Choose between ring and side chain**
$Cl_2$ with $AlCl_3$ or $Fe$ would chlorinate the benzene ring. Here the ring stays untouched and later you get $CH_2Cl$ then $CH_2NH_2$ on the side chain. Chlorination of an alkane side chain is free radical substitution, initiated by homolytic fission of $Cl_2$. That needs UV light.

hints: Examine the tert-butyl group $C_6H_5C(CH_3)_3$, there is no hydrogen on the benzylic carbon itself, so ask which hydrogens can be replaced by $Cl$ under UV light.
walkthrough:
Draw the monochlorinated side chain**
The group attached to the ring is $C(CH_3)_3$. The central carbon joined to the ring has no H, so $Cl$ cannot go there. Under UV light one H on one of the three equivalent $CH_3$ groups is replaced by $Cl$ by free radical substitution. Keep the benzene ring unchanged and draw $C_6H_5C(CH_3)_2CH_2Cl$.

hints: Compare G, $C_6H_5C(CH_3)_2CH_2Cl$, with H, $C_6H_5C(CH_3)_2CH_2NH_2$, and identify what nucleophile must replace $Cl$ by $NH_2$.
Recall the special conditions needed to keep a gaseous nucleophile in solution and to favour the primary amine product.
walkthrough:
Identify the nucleophile**
You are converting $CH_2Cl$ into $CH_2NH_2$. That is nucleophilic substitution where $Cl^-$ leaves and $NH_3$ attacks as the nucleophile to give first the ammonium salt, then the free amine. Use excess concentrated ammonia to minimise further substitution to secondary and tertiary amines.

Hold the gas in solution**
Ammonia is a gas, so at normal heating it would escape. Heating in a sealed tube or under pressure keeps $NH_3$ dissolved and allows the substitution to occur at a good rate.

Final answer: reagents: $NH_3$ (excess concentrated ethanolic ammonia)
conditions: heat in a sealed tube / heat under pressure

hints: Remember a base accepts a proton using the lone pair on nitrogen, so think what ion $C_{10}H_{13}NH_2$ becomes when it gains $H^+$.
walkthrough:
Show proton acceptance on nitrogen**
The $NH_2$ group has a lone pair that can accept $H^+$ from an acid such as $H_3O^+$. Write the equilibrium with the amine protonated to the substituted ammonium ion: $$C_{10}H_{13}NH_2 + H_3O^+ \rightleftharpoons C_{10}H_{13}NH_3^+ + H_2O$$ This demonstrates basic behaviour.

hints: Compare the structures, compound H is a phenyl group separated from $NH_2$ by carbons while phenylamine has $NH_2$ directly on the ring, so consider how available the nitrogen lone pair is in each case versus $NH_3$.
Think about two opposite electronic effects, electron donation by alkyl groups and delocalisation of the lone pair into the benzene ring, and how each affects proton acceptance.
walkthrough:
Rank by lone pair availability**
Basic strength is all about how easily the nitrogen lone pair can be donated to $H^+$. Picture the three: $NH_3$ is the reference, compound H is $C_6H_5C(CH_3)_2CH_2NH_2$, an aliphatic amine with the ring isolated from N, and phenylamine is $C_6H_5NH_2$ with N directly attached to the ring. The order is H strongest, then ammonia, then phenylamine weakest.

Explain why H beats ammonia**
In H the nitrogen is attached to alkyl carbons. Alkyl groups push electrons toward N by the positive inductive effect. That raises electron density on N, the lone pair is held less tightly and donated more easily, so H is a stronger base than $NH_3$.

Explain why phenylamine loses to ammonia**
In phenylamine the lone pair on N overlaps with the pi system of the ring and is delocalised over the benzene ring. Because the lone pair is partly drawn into the ring, it is much less available to bond to $H^+$. Phenylamine is therefore a weaker base than $NH_3$.

Final answer: basicity: compound H > $NH_3$ > phenylamine
in H, alkyl groups are electron donating (+I effect), increasing electron density on N, lone pair more readily donated, so more basic than $NH_3$.
in phenylamine, N lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring, less available to accept $H^+$, so less basic than $NH_3$.
